# Vectors

Vectors are one of the most-used Rust data structures. In other programming
languages, they'd simply be called Arrays, but since Rust operates on a
bit of a lower level, an array in Rust is stored on the stack (meaning it
can't grow or shrink, and the size needs to be known at compile time),
and a Vector is stored in the heap (where these restrictions do not apply).

Vectors are a bit of a later chapter in the book, but we think that they're
useful enough to talk about them a bit earlier. We shall be talking about
the other useful data structure, hash maps, later.

## Further information

- [Storing Lists of Values with Vectors](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch08-01-vectors.html)
- [`iter_mut`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html#method.iter_mut)
- [`map`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.map)
hint:
In Rust, there are two ways to define a Vector.
1. One way is to use the `Vec::new()` function to create a new vector
   and fill it with the `push()` method.
2. The second way is to use the `vec![]` macro and define your elements
   inside the square brackets. This way is simpler when you exactly know
   the initial values.

Check this chapter: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch08-01-vectors.html
of the Rust book to learn more.

Type Option represents an optional value: every Option is either Some and contains a value, or None, and does not.
Option types are very common in Rust code, as they have a number of uses:

- Initial values
- Return values for functions that are not defined over their entire input range (partial functions)

# Traits

A trait is a collection of methods.

Data types can implement traits. To do so, the methods making up the trait are defined for the data type. For example, the `String` data type implements the `From<&str>` trait. This allows a user to write `String::from("hello")`.

In this way, traits are somewhat similar to Java interfaces and C++ abstract classes.

Some additional common Rust traits include:

- `Clone` (the `clone` method)
- `Display` (which allows formatted display via `{}`)
- `Debug` (which allows formatted display via `{:?}`)

Because traits indicate shared behavior between data types, they are useful when writing generics.

# Lifetimes

Lifetimes tell the compiler how to check whether references live long
enough to be valid in any given situation. For example lifetimes say
"make sure parameter 'a' lives as long as parameter 'b' so that the return
value is valid".

They are only necessary on borrows, i.e. references,
since copied parameters or moves are owned in their scope and cannot
be referenced outside. Lifetimes mean that calling code of e.g. functions
can be checked to make sure their arguments are valid. Lifetimes are
restrictive of their callers.

# Type conversions

Rust offers a multitude of ways to convert a value of a given type into another type.

The simplest form of type conversion is a type cast expression. It is denoted with the binary operator `as`. For instance, `println!("{}", 1 + 1.0);` would not compile, since `1` is an integer while `1.0` is a float. However, `println!("{}", 1 as f32 + 1.0)` should compile. The exercise [`using_as`](using_as.rs) tries to cover this.

Rust also offers traits that facilitate type conversions upon implementation. These traits can be found under the [`convert`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/index.html) module.
The traits are the following:

- `From` and `Into` covered in [`from_into`](from_into.rs)
- `TryFrom` and `TryInto` covered in [`try_from_into`](try_from_into.rs)
- `AsRef` and `AsMut` covered in [`as_ref_mut`](as_ref_mut.rs)

Furthermore, the `std::str` module offers a trait called [`FromStr`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/str/trait.FromStr.html) which helps with converting strings into target types via the `parse` method on strings. If properly implemented for a given type `Person`, then `let p: Person = "Mark,20".parse().unwrap()` should both compile and run without panicking.

These should be the main ways ***within the standard library*** to convert data into your desired types.

## Further information

These are not directly covered in the book, but the standard library has a great documentation for it.

- [conversions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/index.html)
- [`FromStr` trait](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/str/trait.FromStr.html)
instructions:
Type casting in Rust is done via the usage of the `as` operator.
Note that the `as` operator is not only used when type casting. It also helps
with renaming imports.

Use the `as` operator to cast one of the operands in the last line of the
`average` function into the expected return type.

# Concurrency & Mutex

In Rust, the type system and ownership model provide strong guarantees against data races. When multiple threads need to share and mutate data simultaneously, Rust provides synchronization primitives in `std::sync`.

- **`Mutex<T>` (Mutual Exclusion)**: Guarantees that only one thread can access the underlying data at any given moment. Access is acquired by calling `.lock().unwrap()`, which returns a `MutexGuard` smart pointer that automatically releases the lock when dropped.
- **`Arc<T>` (Atomic Reference Counting)**: Enables safe shared ownership across multiple thread boundaries (implements `Send` and `Sync` when `T` does). Often combined with `Mutex` as `Arc<Mutex<T>>`.
- **`RwLock<T>` (Reader-Writer Lock)**: Allows multiple threads to read the data concurrently (`.read().unwrap()`), or a single thread to write exclusively (`.write().unwrap()`). Ideal for read-heavy workloads.
- **`Condvar` (Condition Variable)**: Enables threads to wait for a condition to become true without burning CPU cycles in a busy-spin loop. Threads block on `cvar.wait(guard)` and are woken via `cvar.notify_one()` or `cvar.notify_all()`.

## Further Information

- [Shared-State Concurrency (The Rust Book)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch16-03-shared-state.html)
- [std::sync::Mutex Documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)
- [std::sync::RwLock Documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html)
- [std::sync::Condvar Documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Condvar.html)

Multiple threads need to safely mutate a shared counter.
Currently, `counter` is wrapped in an `Arc<u32>`, but `Arc` alone only provides
shared immutable access.

Wrap the counter in a `Mutex` inside the `Arc`, acquire the lock before incrementing,
and get all threads to increment the counter 100 times each.

Execute `rustlings hint mutex1` or use the hint tab for guidance.
hint: Wrap `counter` in `Arc::new(Mutex::new(0))`. Inside each thread, call `let mut num = counter_clone.lock().unwrap(); *num += 1;` to mutate safely.

# Axum Core & Routing

[Axum](https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/) is an ergonomic and modular web application framework built on top of `tokio`, `tower`, and `hyper`.

## Core Concepts

- **`Router`**: Axum's central component for defining URL routes and associating them with HTTP methods (`get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`).
- **Handlers**: Async functions that take extractors as arguments and return types that implement `IntoResponse`.
- **Extractors**: Types that pull data out of the incoming HTTP request:
  - `Path<T>`: Extracts dynamic parameters from the URL path (e.g., `/users/{id}`).
  - `Query<T>`: Deserializes URL query parameters (e.g., `?page=1&limit=10`).
  - `Json<T>`: Parses JSON request bodies into strongly-typed Rust structs using `serde`.
- **State (`State<T>`)**: Allows sharing application state (like connection pools, caches, or `Arc<Mutex<T>>`) across handlers safely.
- **In-Memory Testing with `oneshot`**: Axum routers implement `tower::Service`. You can test your entire application in-memory by sending `axum::http::Request` to `app.oneshot(req).await` without needing a live network port!

## Further Information

- [Official Axum Documentation](https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/)
- [Axum Examples Repository](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum/tree/main/examples)
- [Tower Service Documentation](https://docs.rs/tower/latest/tower/trait.Service.html)

# Axum Middlewares & HTTPS

Middlewares intercept incoming HTTP requests before they reach handlers, and outgoing HTTP responses before they are returned to clients.

## Key Concepts

- **`middleware::from_fn`**: The most ergonomic way to write custom middleware in Axum. An async function with signature `async fn my_middleware(req: Request, next: Next) -> Response`.

- **HTTPS & TLS Security**: Enforcing secure communication through HTTP Strict Transport Security (`HSTS`), preventing clickjacking, and redirecting unencrypted HTTP traffic to HTTPS.

- [Axum Middleware Documentation](https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/middleware/index.html)
- [Tower ServiceBuilder Documentation](https://docs.rs/tower/latest/tower/builder/struct.ServiceBuilder.html)

# WebSockets & Database Tasks

Modern web applications require bidirectional, real-time communication channels (WebSockets) and robust, persistent data stores (PostgreSQL).

## WebSockets in Axum

- **`WebSocketUpgrade` Extractor**: Handles the HTTP protocol upgrade handshake from HTTP/1.1 to the WebSocket protocol.
- **`on_upgrade`**: Spawns an async task to take ownership of the upgraded full-duplex socket stream (`WebSocket`).
- **Stream Processing**: The socket can be split into a sender (`SplitSink`) and receiver (`SplitStream`).
- **Broadcast Channels**: `tokio::sync::broadcast` allows routing real-time messages across multiple connected client streams.

## Database Integration & PostgreSQL

- **Connection Pools in State**: In high-concurrency Axum servers, connection pools (e.g. `sqlx::PgPool` or `tokio_postgres::Client` / pool) are stored inside Axum `State` to reuse established connections.
- **Parameterized SQL Queries**: Never format user inputs into raw SQL strings! Parameterized placeholders (`$1`, `$2`, etc.) prevent SQL injection.
- **Transactions & Atomic State**: Database modifications often involve multiple steps that must succeed or fail as a single atomic unit. If any step fails (e.g. insufficient balance), rolling back prevents inconsistent data states.
- **In-Memory Testing Pattern**: Testing queries, repository interfaces, and state transformations using self-contained in-memory mock repositories and transaction rollbacks allows fast, deterministic verification without requiring a live PostgreSQL daemon.

## Further Information

- [Axum WebSocket Examples](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum/blob/main/examples/websockets/src/main.rs)
- [tokio-postgres Documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio-postgres/latest/tokio_postgres/)
- [PostgreSQL Parameterized Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-prepare.html)
